extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, scientific method, and taxonomy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for constructing precise, complete, and useful scientific terminology and for forming classifications (nomenclature) that best support induction and the discovery/communication of laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision/definiteness of descriptive terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: The language used to record observations must be exact and definite so individual instances can be described with precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give specific, fixed names for parts and properties (examples from botany: calyx, corolla, stamens, pistils; terms for leaf division such as pinnatifid, bipartite). Use classificatory scales where appropriate (Werner's color scale; Mohs hardness scale). The goal is to convey form and structure as exactly as if the part were magnified; include numeric relations when helpful (e.g., siliqua vs silicula defined by length-to-breadth ratio).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness: name common abstractions used in induction
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparison of observed instances yields a new general conception, that abstraction should have a concise name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a brief, fixed term for recurring abstractions so they can be remembered and readily applied in reasoning (examples: 'limit', 'momentum'). Conciseness aids intellectual concentration and recall, facilitating further deduction and discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature: name every Kind (infima species)
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a systematic nomenclature assigning names to every lowest Kind (infima species) with uniform principles for newly discovered kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nomenclature should denote a Kind and be constructed so new species can be named on a consistent principle (examples: Linnæan system for plants/animals; systematic chemical nomenclature). Where absent (e.g., mineralogy), lack of systematic nomenclature retards progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology vs nomenclature distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminology: descriptive terms for attributes; Nomenclature: systematic names for Kinds/species. Both are essential components of a philosophical language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terminology to convey attributes (e.g., lanceolate, serrate) and nomenclature to denote the Kinds (e.g., Viola odorata). Recognize the different roles and construct each accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must supply discriminating characters for nomenclature terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Words in a nomenclature carry connotation as well as denotation; the set of characters used to discriminate a Kind constitutes a true definition of the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though a nomenclature term denotes a Kind, its meaning can and should be unfolded by enumerating discriminating characters; the definition and the form of the word together constitute its signification (example discussed: 'peroxide of iron' and 'Viola odorata').

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix and preserve meanings for frequent and important terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a concept is repeatedly used, fix its sense by consistently using the same word in the same meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stability of terms (e.g., botanical nomenclature fixed by Linnaeus) sheds clearness and precision over a science; avoid changing the meaning capriciously and use fixed names to keep ideas before the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concise names to aid thought and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: A compact name promotes remembrance, suggests the definition, and keeps the abstraction constantly before the intellectual attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invent or select short, apt names for new distinctions to 'nail them down' in thought (examples: 'Delegation is not Representation' as a compact distinction). Concision aids the persistence and spread of original thoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical use of language except where safe (mechanical-resistance principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: When subjects permit mechanical operations safely (e.g., arithmetic/algebra), language should favor mechanical use; otherwise, the language should hinder merely mechanical application without understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic/symbolical notation is exemplary for numerical reasoning because it intentionally permits manipulation without attending to meaning. For non-mathematical subjects, design language to keep meaning always present so users cannot reason by rote with unintelligible counters. Anti-pattern: treating non-mathematical terminology like algebraic symbols and reasoning without continuous reference to the phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbolical/mathematical language where problems reduce to numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: For domains reducible to relations between numbers, algebraic notation (compact unmeaning signs) is ideal because it enables purely mechanical manipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt symbolical shorthand when the investigation truly depends on numerical relations; only after reduction to equation does it become safe to dismiss concrete meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed meaning in word-formation to prevent semantic decay
rubrics_metrics.description: Form words so their derivation and analogy keep alive the consciousness of what they signify, thereby resisting the tendency of words to lose meaning through use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer native-root compounding systems (examples: German, Greek) where derivatives transparently relate to primitives. Use fixed analogies in word-formation so the relation between primitive and derivative remains clear. This reduces the chance that terms will become meaningless counters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain continual acquaintance with real phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must habitually contemplate the phenomena themselves rather than living exclusively among formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure mode: applying formulas without verifying whether other laws or peculiarities intervene; also progressive loss of meaning in the formulas. Keep refreshing acquaintance with real cases to preserve the connection between words/formulae and the phenomena they describe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification should order ideas to maximize recall and law-discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification is a contrivance to order mental ideas so as to best conduce to remembrance and to the ascertainment of laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange objects into groups and order those groups to give greatest command over acquired knowledge and to lead most directly to acquiring more. Classification's main aim is cognitive utility for induction, not merely convenient labeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer properties that are causes or sure marks when choosing classification criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The properties used for grouping should, if possible, be causes of many other properties or reliable marks of them, because such properties yield more and more important general propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes are preferable because they are the most direct and useful marks; when causes can't be diagnostic, select prominent effects that serve as marks of the underlying cause. Avoid basing classification on properties that yield few useful generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor natural (scientific/philosophical) classifications over artificial ones
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural classification groups objects that share many and important properties, enabling numerous and important general propositions; artificial/technical classifications are based on arbitrarily selected single circumstances and are less useful for induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a classification by the number and importance of properties common to its members. Beware systems that group objects by trivial, easily perceived traits (e.g., Tournefort's corolla-shape or Linnæan stamen counts) if those traits are not indicative of other shared properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification must consider all real objects and their affinities
rubrics_metrics.description: To properly constitute any class, one must consider the general division of the whole of nature and the place of the object within that whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A family or class should be formed in reference to the complete set of existing objects with any degree of affinity; local or isolated grouping without regard to the broader system risks incoherence and misplacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing classification on simple perceptible properties alone
rubrics_metrics.description: While simple perceptible properties are tempting as foundations for classification, they often fail to group objects in ways useful for scientific generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example anti-patterns: Tournefort's corolla-shape system and the Linnæan stamen/pistil count—they make grouping easy but rarely produce useful general propositions. Prefer properties that indicate many other common traits.
